bio.en: Brendan Foody is CEO and co-founder of Mercor, the fastest-growing company in history to reach $500M in revenue (in 17 months) and the youngest unicorn founder, building a marketplace for AI training labor.
bio.zh: Brendan Foody 是 Mercor 的 CEO 兼联合创始人，该公司是史上最快达到 5 亿美元收入（仅 17 个月）的公司，他也是最年轻的独角兽创始人，正在打造一个 AI 训练劳动力的市场。

summary.en: Brendan explains the rise of “evals”—measuring model capabilities—as possibly the biggest business opportunity in history, with Mercor supplying extraordinary professionals to top AI labs. He covers what product-market fit looks like for this new category, the tenets that enabled such extreme growth, and what evaluators actually do day to day. The conversation also explores which skills and jobs will last longest with AI and why he doesn't expect AGI soon.
summary.zh: Brendan 解释了“评估”（evals，即衡量模型能力）的崛起——可能是史上最大的商业机会——Mercor 正为顶尖 AI 实验室提供顶尖专业人才。他讲述了这一新品类产品市场匹配的样子、支撑极端增长的原则，以及评估者每天实际在做什么。对话还探讨了在 AI 时代哪些技能和工作最持久，以及他为何不认为 AGI 会很快到来。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: We grew from 1 to 400 million in revenue run rate in 16 months, fastest ascent in history.
turns.zh: 我们在16个月内将收入增长率从1百万提升至4亿，是史上最快的增长速度。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: The market is bound by the amount of things where humans can do something that models can't. The lab's primary bottleneck to improve models is how they can effectively have some way of measuring what success looks like for the model.
turns.zh: 市场受限于人类能做而模型做不了的事物数量。实验室提升模型能力的主要瓶颈在于如何有效衡量模型的成功标准。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Exactly. So fastest ascent in history, which is an exciting statistic we're very proud of.
turns.zh: 没错。这是史上最快的提升速度，这是一个令人振奋的数据，我们为此深感自豪。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So something big is happening here. Why is this so valuable? What is going on here? So it's just to try to summarize what you guys do simply is you help hire people for labs to help them train their models, and you help them find not just generalist labor, but experts, helping them with very specific gaps in the model's knowledge.
turns.zh: 好的。所以这里正在发生一件大事。为什么这如此重要？到底怎么回事？简单来说，就是你们帮助实验室招聘人才，协助他们训练模型，不仅提供通用人才，还招募专家，填补模型知识中的特定空白。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Yeah, precisely. And so it really ties to your first question around the era of evals that's framing all of this, which is that the lab's primary bottleneck to being able to improve models is how they can effectively have some way of measuring what success looks like for the model, both to use it as the eval for the tests that they're measuring their progress against, as well as the verifiers in an RL environment to then reward the model, improve capabilities, et cetera. And they need this across every domain for every capability that models don't know how to use. And the wealthiest companies in the world are willing to spend whatever it takes to improve model capabilities where Mercor is sitting at the forefront and the primary bottleneck.
turns.zh: 是的，正是如此。这与你们最初提到的评估时代紧密相连，即实验室在提升模型能力方面的主要瓶颈在于如何有效衡量模型的成功标准——无论是作为测试评估的基准，还是在强化学习环境中用于奖励模型、提升能力等。在每个领域，每项模型未掌握的技能上，他们都需要这样的评估体系。全球顶尖公司愿意不惜一切代价提升模型能力，而Mercor正处于这一领域的前沿。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, what are these people actually doing? So what's an example of a kind of person that is sought after? And then what are they doing sitting there at the computer?
turns.zh: 好的，这些人才具体做些什么？能举个例子说明一下被招聘的对象是什么样的？他们坐在电脑前做些什么？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Effectively, the market is bound by the amount of things where humans can do something that models can't. So I'll make that very concrete. Say you have a model that you want to write a red line for a contract in the way that a lawyer would, and it makes a handful of mistakes, misses a bunch of key points in doing so. What you could do is have a lawyer create a rubric similar to how a professor might create a rubric to create a deliverable for what are the things we want the model to be able to do? (00:13:50): So it can effectively score that, right? Plus however much of it identifies this or XYZ key point. And that's really the foundation to measuring what does progress look like for models? Is this model achieving the capabilities that these professionals want? As well as how do we use this as training data to reward and to reinforce a lot of the capabilities that people want models to achieve.
turns.zh: 实际上，市场受限于人类能做而模型做不了的任务数量。举个具体例子：假设你想让模型像律师那样给合同写红线，但它犯了几个错误，遗漏了关键点。你可以让律师创建一个类似教授评分标准的评分体系，列出模型应该具备的能力要素。这样模型就能根据这些标准进行评分，对吧？同时评分能反馈出模型在哪些关键点上达标了。这正是衡量模型进步的核心——模型是否达到了专业人士设定的标准？以及如何利用这些数据作为训练素材，奖励和强化模型所需的能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so they're essentially writing evals just to connect it back to original conversation.
turns.zh: 好的，他们本质上是在编写评估标准，以此回归到最初的讨论。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Exactly. Well, that's an interesting thing is everyone talks about RL environment. I feel like the two hot button things are like RL environments and evals, but one thing like Andrej Karpathy's tweeted out about a bunch is there's not actually a nuance. It's in the data type. It's more just a different semantic way of describing what it's being used for. But ultimately, it's just some stasis point for how do you measure what good looks like? And you can use that either as the benchmark to the sales collateral, as Sarah was saying, to say, here is why are models the best model in the world and here's the capabilities that we've been working towards, or you can use it on the post-training side to reward certain model trajectories and achieve those capabilities.
turns.zh: 没错。有趣的是，所有人都谈论强化学习环境。但安德烈·卡帕西（Andrej Karpathy）在推特上多次提到，关键不在于环境本身，而在于数据类型。这只是描述用途的不同语义方式。但归根结底，核心问题在于如何衡量成功标准？你可以将其作为销售材料的基准，比如莎拉（Sarah）提到的——展示模型为何是全球最佳，并列出我们努力达成的能力目标；也可以在训练后阶段用于奖励特定模型路径，助力实现这些能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So say this lawyer, this person is writing, "Here's what a great red line contract looks like and here's the rubric of what excellent is." Then are they also providing data, like actual examples of red line documents as a part of that?
turns.zh: 好的。所以这位律师，写道“这就是一份优秀的红线合同应该有的样子”，以及“优秀的标准是什么”。那么，他们是否还提供了数据，比如实际的红线文件示例作为补充？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: They may. The data landscape historically has included two kinds of data. The first is supervised fine-tuning data, which is input/output. When people think about fine-tuning in the historical sense, that's what it is. The second is RLHF where the model will generate a couple of examples. We'll choose which is the most popular example. (00:15:43): What everyone is generally moving towards is reinforcement learning from AI feedback instead of human feedback where you have instead the human defined some sort of success criteria, some way to measure that. And examples in code, it could be a unit test. We can scalably measure success and other domains that could be a rubric. And then you use that to incentivize model capabilities. And it's far more scalable and data-efficient, and so that's why a lot of the broader trend in the market across the board is moving towards RLHF to both eval models as well as improved capabilities.
turns.zh: 有可能。数据格局历来包含两种类型的数据。第一种是监督微调数据，即输入/输出数据。在传统意义上，当人们谈到微调时，指的就是这种数据。第二种是RLHF（强化学习与人类反馈），模型会生成几个示例，然后我们选择最受欢迎的那个。（00:15:43）：目前市场上的普遍趋势是转向基于AI反馈的强化学习，而非依赖人类反馈。传统上，人类会定义一些成功标准和衡量方法。例如，代码中的示例可能是一项单元测试。我们可以可扩展地衡量成功与否，以及其他领域可能采用的评分标准。然后利用这些标准来激励模型能力。这更加可扩展且节省数据，因此市场上广泛的趋势是转向RLHF，既用于模型评估，也用于能力提升。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I had one of the co-founders of Anthropic on. He said exactly the same thing. That's what they've done at Anthropic, is move towards AI-driven reinforcement learning. (00:16:32): So essentially, if I can understand this correctly, I'm the lay person here trying to understand this on behalf of the audience. So essentially a lawyer is like, "Here's what correct looks like for redlining," and then it's AI is just on its own almost, just like, "I'm going to try to get this. I'm going to try to improve on this and I know if I'm heading the right direction based on this eval/rubric I've been given."
turns.zh: 我邀请了Anthropic的联合创始人。他也说了同样的话。这就是他们在Anthropic所做的，转向AI驱动的强化学习。（00:16:32）：所以基本上，如果我理解正确的话，我是作为外行来代表听众理解这个的。所以律师会说，“这就是红线工作的正确样子”，而AI几乎是自行运作的，就像，“我要尝试改进这个，根据给定的评估/评分标准，我知道自己是否朝着正确的方向前进。”

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Exactly. Applying all of the criteria of what good looks like similar to how the TA might apply the professor's criteria of does the student's response meet this criteria or this criteria plus however many planes, et cetera.
turns.zh: 完全正确。应用所有标准来判断什么是优秀的，就像助教可能会应用教授的标准一样，学生是否符合这个或那个标准，以及多少层级等等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome, okay. Let me shift to talking about the broader labor market here. So there's two parts to this question as we talk about this. One is just how long will we need to do this? You guys grew so incredibly fast. Is there a point of like, "Okay, we don't need humans. We're tapped out." So let's start there and then I'll ask a broader question.
turns.zh: 太棒了，好的。让我转到更广泛的劳动力市场话题上。当我们讨论这个问题时，主要有两个方面。首先是我们需要这样做多久？你们发展得非常快。是否会达到一个临界点，比如“好吧，我们不需要人类了。我们已经用尽了所有资源。” 所以让我们先从这个问题入手，然后我会再问一个更广泛的问题。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: So the key question is how long there's going to be things in the economy that humans can do that AI can't do? And I think there's certainly a bucket of people that say we're going to have superintelligence within three years and humans won't play a role in the economy. And that's one school of thought. (00:17:46): Our perspective is very different. Our perspective is that these models are extraordinary and automating a lot of things very quickly, but there's a lot of things that they're horrible at. Even still, it can't schedule time on my calendar. It can't draft emails for me. It can't use basic tools. And we need evals for everything. For everything that the models can't do, we need evals for the tool use, evals for the long horizon reasoning. (00:18:12): Imagine in 10 years when we want models to be able to go out and build a startup for 30 days. We need evals for that to effectively reward it. And I think that that road to improving models will last for as long as there is anything in the economy that humans can do which models can't and be a huge portion of what the future of work looks like. And so our mission is creating the future of work, and I think that this is a really exciting industry and giving us a glimpse into the direction that everything is headed towards.
turns.zh:
关键问题在于，在经济领域，人类能做而人工智能做不了的事情还会持续多久？我认为肯定有很多人声称，我们将在三年内拥有超智能，人类将不再在经济中发挥作用。这是一种观点。但我们的看法截然不同。这些模型确实非凡，正在迅速自动化许多任务，但它们在很多方面表现糟糕。即便如此，它们仍无法在我的日历上安排时间、为我起草邮件、使用基本工具。我们需要对所有事情进行评估。对于模型无法完成的每一项任务，我们都需要评估工具使用情况、评估长远规划能力。

（00:18:12）想象一下，10年后我们希望模型能够在30天内创办一家初创公司。我们需要为此制定有效的奖励机制。这条提升模型的道路将持续下去，只要经济中还有人类能做而模型做不了的事情，这将成为未来工作的核心组成部分。因此，我们的使命是创造未来的工作模式，我认为这是一个非常令人兴奋的行业，它让我们得以一窥未来发展的大方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's this tweet that you retweeted that I want to ask you about. "If you really think about it, we were put on Earth to create reinforcement learning training data for labs."
turns.zh: 你转发的那条推文我想问问你。“如果你仔细想想，我们被放在地球上就是为了给实验室提供强化学习训练数据的。”

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What does that mean to you? What is this person implying? And it's basically what you're saying is we're just helping train models.
turns.zh: 这对你意味着什么？这个人暗示的是什么？基本上你的意思是我们只是在帮助训练模型。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: It speaks to conversations I've had with a lot of researchers and executives at top labs, which is that it's highly likely that the entire economy will become an aural environment machine, building out all of these worlds and contexts for us to then have rubrics or other kinds of verifiers. And that is really exciting in so many ways. (00:19:32): Because I think let's draw an analog to other revolutions where when we had the industrial revolution, everyone was freaking out about losing their jobs, but there was this whole new class of jobs of how do we build the machines? How do we have knowledge work? How do we create everything new? And I think that the narrative in AI over the last three years has almost entirely been one of job displacement, right? Sure, there's ChatGPT is growing fast and it's very cool that everyone loves using it, but from an economic standpoint, people talking a lot about job displacement. But very few companies and people have talked about this new category of jobs that's being created and what that's going to mean and how people can prepare and upskill for that. And I think that the most exciting thing possible is creating that future of how do humans fit into the economy and how will that evolve over time?
turns.zh:
这让我想起了我与顶尖实验室的许多研究人员和高管进行的讨论，即整个经济很可能成为一个虚拟环境机器，为我们构建所有这些世界和场景，然后我们可以制定评分标准或其他验证方法。这在很多方面都非常令人兴奋。

（00:19:32）因为我认为，我们可以将其与其他革命进行类比。工业革命时期，每个人都为失业而感到恐慌，但随之而来的是一个全新的就业类别——如何制造机器？如何开展知识型工作？如何创造新事物？我认为过去三年的AI叙事几乎完全围绕着就业替代展开。当然，ChatGPT发展迅速，人们喜欢使用它，但从经济角度来看，人们谈论的更多是就业替代。但很少有公司和个人谈论正在创造的新就业类别、这将意味着什么以及人们如何为此做好准备和提升技能。我认为最令人兴奋的事情就是创造未来，即人类如何融入经济，以及这种融入将如何随时间演变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I talk to a lot of people about just what should I be studying? Where should I be getting better? People in school right now are just like, "What is even going to be valuable in the future?" You're at the center of a lot of just what jobs are most in demand, how hiring is evolving. So let me just ask you a very concrete question. What jobs do you think will remain in the future/what skills are still worth investing in for younger people, especially?
turns.zh: 我经常和很多人讨论这个问题：我到底该学什么？我该在哪些方面提升自己？如今在校学生总在问：“未来什么才有价值？”你身处诸多热门职位的核心，深知招聘趋势如何演变。让我直截了当地问你：你认为哪些职位在未来会持续存在？哪些技能对年轻人而言仍值得投入精力培养？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: In terms of jobs, I would respond with a category of things that have very elastic demand are going to be super exciting. Because when we make people 10 times more productive, we'll build 10 times, if not 100 times as much software as an example. And so I think the product managers that can now do so much more are going to be extremely well-positioned. And so far as the skills, I think it's people that can leverage AI to do whatever their day-to-day workflows are. (00:21:16): I have had a couple conversations with teachers where they get my thoughts on how they should be assessing their students because we originally started out curating all of these AI interviews and assessments for people and have thought about this immensely. And what we realized is that you don't want to fight against them using the models. It's similar to when the calculator came out, you don't want to give people all of this arithmetic work of how do you get them to do it and not use the calculator. You want to tell them, "Use the tools and let's see what you can do." (00:21:49): And so we'll give people interviews where we say, "Use ChatGPT and Kodak. Use Claude code. Use whatever tool cursor and whatever tools are available to build a website and let's see what product you're able to build in an hour." And so I think that I give that an example in so far as talent assessment because I think it pertains also to the skills that people should be honing in on of how can they leverage this technology to do so much more in whatever industry or vertical they're operating in.
turns.zh: 谈到职位选择，我会提到需求弹性极大的领域，这类职位将极具吸引力。因为当我们能让人们的生产力提高十倍时，举例来说，我们开发的软件量就会翻十倍甚至百倍。因此，善于利用人工智能优化日常工作流程的产品经理，将在未来占据极佳的竞争优势。就技能培养而言，我认为关键在于让人们能借助AI技术提升效率。（00:21:16）：我曾与多位教师交流，分享如何评估学生学习成果的见解。最初我们为用户整理AI面试题和评估工具时，深有感触：不应试图用模型去对抗人工智能。这就好比计算器问世时，人们不应强迫学生费力计算，而是应教会他们如何高效使用工具。（00:21:49）：因此，我们设计的面试题会要求使用ChatGPT、Kodak、Claude等工具，构建网站时，会让参与者在一小时内完成产品设计。这些例子充分说明了人才评估的理念——关键在于如何利用现有技术，提升各行业从业者的价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you talk about elastic, being elastic, is it generalists being good at just a bunch of different things, or what do you say? What do you mean when you think elastic?
turns.zh: 当你谈到弹性时，具体指的是通才型人才精通多项技能，还是另有深意？你所说的弹性究竟指什么？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: So I more mean how much capacity for demand there is in that industry. So I'll give a couple of examples. In accounting, I think realistically we only need so much accounting in the world. Maybe there's areas where we can do more and that'll be good, but it doesn't feel like the world needs 100 times more accounting. (00:22:46): On the other hand, in software development, I think we can ship 100 times more features for our products, move 100 times faster, build so much more. There's just it feels like there's unlimited demand for the industry. And I think Mark Andreessen tweeted about this recently, that software is the most elastic industry of all where when we increase productivity, there's so much more that will be built. And it's definitely characteristic of a lot of other domains as well. And so I would focus on those domains where if we make everyone 10 times more productive, that'll increase demand, not reduce it.
turns.zh: 我更关注该行业的需求弹性。我举几个例子：在会计领域，全球对会计服务的需求实际上有限。当然，有些领域可能存在提升空间，但全球对会计服务的需求绝非百倍增长。（00:22:46）：相反，在软件开发领域，我们能为产品交付百倍多的功能，开发速度提升百倍，创造的价值也将指数级增长。马克·安德森近期发文指出，软件是弹性最强的行业——当生产力提升时，创造的价值将呈几何级数增长。这同样适用于许多其他领域。因此，我建议重点关注那些当我们提升全员生产力时，需求会随之增长而非缩减的领域。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So you're in the bucket of learn to code, still useful as a skill. You take computer science. And so in terms of elastic categories of jobs, sounds like engineering, product management is in that bucket. Great. A lot of people listening to this are PMs. What else, like design users? I don't know. What else do you feel is in that bucket from what you've seen?
turns.zh: 好的。所以你属于“学会编程”这一类别，这项技能仍然很有用。你学的是计算机科学。就弹性就业类别而言，工程、产品管理等领域似乎都属于这一类。太棒了。很多听众都是产品经理。还有什么别的领域呢？比如设计师或用户体验专家？我不太确定。根据你的观察，你觉得还有哪些领域属于这一类？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Yeah, I think that there's a lot of things where the whole value chain of building companies has a lot of these variable costs, even large portions of operations or consulting. Imagine if we could have 10 times as many McKinsey consultants, what would be possible in so far as the research we could do, the analysis, et cetera. But I think the companies and people that are going to succeed are those that lean into this narrative of abundance of how do we do so much more rather than fighting back against it of how do we try to stop displacement.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为整个公司建设的价值链中有很多可变成本，甚至包括大量运营或咨询业务。想象一下，如果我们能增加10倍的麦肯锡顾问数量，我们能在研究、分析等领域做多少事情。但我认为成功的公司和个人会顺应这种充足资源的趋势——思考如何做更多事情，而不是与之抗争，试图阻止被替代的局面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So along those lines, I think about your second bucket, which is the people that will be most successful. It's not like a specific skill, but it's being good with AI, using AI to become better at what you're already doing. This reminds me of Elon's whole thing with Neuralink, which I don't know if this is how we put it, but the way I've always heard it is you wanted to build Neuralink because in the future when AGI and superintelligence is around, we need a way to compete and the best way to compete is plug our brains into a superintelligence so we have a chance. And it feels like that's what AI is. Getting good at AI tools is essentially is having this super superpower.
turns.zh: 所以顺着这个思路，我想到了第二个类别，即最有可能成功的人。这不是特定的技能，而是善于运用AI，将AI融入现有工作中。这让我想起埃隆·马斯克关于Neuralink的想法。我不知道我们是否应该这样表述，但我一直听到的是，他想开发Neuralink是因为未来，当通用人工智能和超级智能出现时，我们需要一种竞争方式，而最佳竞争手段就是将大脑接入超级智能，这样我们才有机会。感觉这就是AI的本质。精通AI工具本质上就是拥有这种超级能力。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Figuring out how to leverage them and incorporate it will definitely be of paramount importance.
turns.zh: 如何利用和整合这些工具无疑将至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It just comes back to this almost cliche quote now. It's, "AI won't replace you. People that are really good with AI will replace you."
turns.zh: 这又回到了那句近乎陈词滥调的名言：“AI不会取代你。但真正精通AI的人会取代你。”

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: I think it's totally spot on. And I've definitely seen this at the enterprise level as well where there's certain enterprises we talk to that are almost fearful not wanting to engage, not wanting to eval their businesses because that'll provide the evidence that their value chain is being automated. And there's others that... Literally some of the most recognized sophisticated Fortune 500 businesses that have this mentality and there's others that are leaning into it of if we have the ability to do 10 or 100 times more, what will that mean and how do we lean into that future? Because there's so many things that are going to change over the next 10 years, and I think those are the kinds of businesses that are going to be successful.
turns.zh: 我认为这完全正确。我在企业层面也确实见过这种情况。我们接触的一些企业几乎心怀恐惧，不愿参与评估业务，因为这会暴露出他们的价值链正在被自动化的事实。而另一些企业……甚至一些最知名的成熟《财富》500强企业也抱有这种心态，还有一些企业则积极迎接挑战：如果我们能做10倍或100倍的工作，意义何在？我们该如何拥抱这个未来？因为未来10年将有太多东西发生变化，我认为这类企业才最有可能成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's talk about labor markets more broadly. You guys, so it's interesting though. You started not feeding people to AI labs, not training models. It was just like help people find jobs, help companies hire, and then you're like, "Oh wow, this whole opportunity." You have this really interesting view on the future of just labor markets and hiring. Talk about that.
turns.zh: 让我们更广泛地谈谈劳动力市场。各位，这很有趣。你们最初不是为AI实验室提供人才，也不是训练模型。而是帮助人们找工作，帮助公司招聘，然后你们突然发现这是一个巨大的机遇。你们对劳动力市场和招聘的未来有着非常有趣的见解。请谈谈这一点。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Yeah, it's interesting. I remember when we started the company, as I mentioned, we were 19, and just had this gut intuition that it felt so wildly inefficient that labor markets are so disaggregated. And what I mean by that is when we would hire someone internationally, they would apply to a dozen jobs. When we as a company in the Bay Area were considering candidates, we would consider a fraction of a percent of candidates that were available in the market. And the reason for that is that there was this matching problem that everyone's solving manually where they'll manually review resumes, they'll manually conduct interviews, and manually decide who to hire. But when we're able to automate that matching problem at the cost of software, it makes way for this global unified labor market that every candidate applies to and every company hires from facilitating a perfect flow of information in the economy. (00:27:08): And I think that that future is undoubtedly what we're heading towards, but what we've realized over time is that the nature of work is also changing dramatically. And part of building that future over a 10-year time horizon is creating that future of work and all of the more tactical things we do and building these incredible data sets across evals and RL environments for our customers.
turns.zh: 是啊，这确实很有趣。我记得我们创办公司时，正如我之前提到的，我们当时才19岁，只是凭着一种直觉，觉得劳动力市场如此割裂，效率极低，这实在太不合理了。我的意思是，当我们在国际上招聘员工时，他们得申请十几份工作。而当我们湾区的公司考虑候选人时，能筛选到的市场上可用候选人比例微乎其微。这背后的原因是，所有人都在手动解决一个匹配问题——他们要手动审查简历、进行面试、决定录用谁。但当我们能通过软件自动化解决这个匹配问题时，就为全球统一的劳动力市场铺平了道路。每个候选人都能申请到职位，每个公司都能从中招聘，信息在经济体系中得以完美流通。（00:27:08）：我认为这个未来无疑是我们正在朝着的方向发展，但随着时间推移，我们意识到工作的性质也在发生着巨大变化。在未来10年的时间维度里构建这个未来，关键在于打造未来的工作模式，以及我们所做的所有更具策略性的工作，比如为客户在评估和强化学习环境中构建这些令人惊叹的数据集。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I've seen in how hiring has changed, I'm doing research on this with a partner, Gnome, it's so much easier to apply for companies that everyone's just applying now, to hundreds of companies. AI is just making it easy to adjust their resumes and cover letters and make it feel like, "Oh, I applied to more of course very specifically, but it was one of 100 places." And then on the flip side, hiring managers are getting flooded with applications and so now they need AI to filter. So even if we didn't want to get to this place, we're almost being pushed into this direction of so much volume on both sides. We need something really smart at filtering and helping us hire and select, and this is exactly what you guys have been building for a long time.
turns.zh: 从招聘方式的变化来看，我和合作伙伴Gnome正在研究这一问题。现在申请公司变得容易得多，每个人都在申请数百家公司。人工智能让他们能轻松调整简历和求职信，让人感觉：“哦，我申请了更多公司，当然是针对特定职位的，但只是100个职位中的一个。”而另一方面，招聘经理们则被大量申请淹没，因此现在他们需要人工智能来筛选。即使我们不想走到这一步，双方巨大的招聘量也几乎把我们推向了这个方向。我们需要一些真正智能的工具来筛选和帮助我们招聘及选拔人才，而这正是你们长期以来一直在构建的。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Precisely, yeah. And the fascinating thing a lot of people ask, do we think about ourselves as a labor marketplace or do we think about ourselves as a data company? And I think that the reason it's an interesting question is our realization on from what the labs need is that they actually need a labor marketplace. They actually need these exceptionally high caliber people. And of course we'll layer on some project management and some software platform associated with it. But the really core thing that they want is how do they find these extraordinary professionals across all of these different domains that can measure model capabilities and work to build that future work together?
turns.zh: 确实如此。很多人会问一个有趣的问题：我们认为自己是劳动力市场平台，还是数据公司？我认为这个问题之所以有趣，是因为我们从实验室需求中意识到，他们实际上需要一个劳动力市场平台。他们需要这些极高水准的人才。当然，我们会为此添加一些项目管理和相关软件平台。但他们真正核心的需求是如何在所有不同领域找到这些杰出专业人才，这些人才能够评估模型能力，并共同开创未来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This episode is brought to you by Enterpret. Enterpret is a customer intelligence platform used by our leading CXN product orgs like Canva, Notion, Perplexity, Strava, Hinge, and Linear to leverage the voice of the customer and build best in class products. Enterpret unifies all customer conversations in real time, from Gong recordings to Zendesk tickets to Twitter threads, and makes it available for your team for analysis and for action. (00:29:21): What makes Enterpret unique is its ability to build and update a customer-specific knowledge graph that provides the most granular and accurate categorization of all customer feedback and connects that customer feedback to critical metrics like revenue and CSAT. If modernizing your voice of customer program to a generational upgrade is a 2025 priority, customer-centric industry leaders like Canva, Notion, Perplexity, and Linear, reach out to the team at enterpret.com/lenny. That's E-N-T-E-R-P-R-E-T.com/lenny. (00:29:55): Going back to just how this all works and what you guys do for models, I was talking to a friend who had an ankle sprain or his foot was hurting and he got an x-ray and he fed the x-ray into ChatGPT and then asked him, "Give me this specific x-ray." And it's like, "Okay, sure." And then it gave him, "Here's what you have." And he was talking to me, he's like, "What is out there on the internet that trained this model to know this stuff?" And I was like, "No, it's actually somebody sitting there helping the model understand this. Once they recognize, it doesn't fully understand this. Humans are actually helping them learn these things."
turns.zh: 本期节目由Enterpret赞助。Enterpret是一家客户智能平台，许多领先的客户体验管理（CXN）产品团队，如Canva、Notion、Perplexity、Strava、Hinge和Linear，正在使用该平台，充分利用客户的声音，打造一流的产品。Enterpret实时整合所有客户对话数据——从Gong录音到Zendesk工单，再到Twitter讨论——并将其呈现给团队，供分析和决策之用。（00:29:21）：Enterpret的独特之处在于，它能够构建和更新客户专属知识图谱，对所有客户反馈进行最细粒度、最精准的分类，并将这些反馈与营收和客户满意度（CSAT）等关键指标关联起来。如果将客户反馈计划升级至2025年的标准，Canva、Notion、Perplexity和Linear等以客户为中心的行业领导者，请访问enterpret.com/lenny联系我们。网址是E-N-T-E-R-P-R-E-T.com/lenny。（00:29:55）：回到模型如何运作的问题。我有个朋友脚踝扭伤了，去拍了X光片，把X光片结果输入ChatGPT，然后问它：“给我看看这张X光片。” 它回答：“好的，没问题。”接着给出诊断结果。他问我：“网上哪里训练了这个模型，让它能识别这些内容？” 我回答：“不，其实是有人手动帮助模型理解这些内容。一旦模型识别后，它并不能完全理解这些知识。人类在帮助它学习这些东西。”

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Exactly. Well, so the way it works, at least what most people's understanding is there's a lot of complexity in how the models work, is that pre-training gets a lot of the knowledge into the model of what are all the different things that see into the world. And then post-training and reinforcement learning is for all of the reasoning of what are the pieces of knowledge that are accurate, what are inaccurate, and what to prioritize at any given time to make a decision. And so behind that, there would've been radiologists that worked on the post-training data set to create some stasis point for here's the diagnosis and rewards and penalties associated with it. And it's really the quality of those people that went into the quality of the decision and recommendation that ChatGPT ultimately made.
turns.zh: 没错。至少大多数人理解的是，模型的工作机制非常复杂。预训练阶段会让模型掌握大量关于世界的不同事物的知识。而后续的训练和强化学习阶段，则用于处理这些知识的准确性问题，以及在特定时刻优先处理哪些信息以做出决策。因此，在后续阶段，肯定有放射科医生参与到训练数据集中，为诊断结果和相关奖惩机制设定标准。最终，ChatGPT所做出的决策和推荐的质量，实际上取决于这些专家的专业水平。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's actually follow that, right, because that's really interesting and I don't know how many people understand it. I understand it. So the work that you do and these experts do is post-training. It's not feeding data into the model that it's trained on. It's, "We have this model GPT-5. Now here's all the things that's missing. Let's add to it."
turns.zh: 那我们具体来探讨一下，因为这真的很有趣，我不知道有多少人能理解。我能理解。所以你和这些专家的工作属于后续训练阶段。不是把数据输入到训练过的模型中，而是：“我们现在有GPT-5模型。现在这里缺少一些内容，让我们来补充吧。”

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Exactly, yeah. It's really unlocking, allowing the model to focus on all the right tokens, from pre-training all the right things in model context, up weighting the effective reasoning chains to enable the models to reason better in a more generalized way.
turns.zh: 没错，确实是在解锁模型，让它专注于所有正确的标记，从模型上下文中预训练所有正确的内容，到对有效推理链进行加权，帮助模型以更通用的方式更好地进行推理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the scale of people just working on the stuff. It's like thousands, tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands?
turns.zh: 参与这项工作的团队规模有多大？是数千人、数万人还是数十万人？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Tens of thousands at any given time, hundreds of thousands more generally. It's huge. And the most exciting thing is that it's growing really quickly. I think that to your question also about the competitive landscape, historically there were all these crowdsourcing companies that would get these super high volumes of low-skilled people. I think Scale and Surge were the primary companies that pioneered that industry. And then in this transition to higher-skilled labor, what people realized is that actually you can go a lot further with just getting higher caliber people even in smaller amounts initially, and now subsequently scaling that back up once they're able to meet the quality bar. (00:32:35): And I think that there's a bunch of companies that after our success and very rapid revenue growth that started early last year have chased after that, which makes sense. And seeing that the market was changing very quickly, we were taking off, and trying to pursue a similar thesis on the market.
turns.zh: 任何时候都有数万人，总体而言则有数十万人。这规模非常庞大。最令人兴奋的是，这个行业正以极快的速度发展。我想您之前提到的竞争格局问题——历史上，曾有许多众包公司招募大量低技能人员。Scale和Surge是该领域的先驱企业。如今，在向高技能劳动力转型过程中，人们意识到，即使最初只招募少量高素质人才，也能取得显著成效，待他们达到质量标准后，再逐步扩大规模。（00:32:35）：我认为，自去年初我们成功并实现收入快速增长后，许多公司纷纷效仿这一模式，这合乎情理。鉴于市场变化迅速，我们正顺势而为，试图在市场中探索类似的机遇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting. There's always been these companies, AlphaSights and GLG, that did this before AI or is paid to connect to an expert and ask them questions about stuff. And essentially, okay, it turns out this is really useful for models. We don't need the person in the middle.
turns.zh: 这很有意思。早在人工智能出现之前，就有AlphaSights和GLG这样的公司，通过付费连接专家并向他们提问来获取信息。本质上，现在发现这对模型非常有用，我们不再需要中间人。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Exactly, yeah. Well, but one core difference is that AlphaSights would generally be a one-off call versus a lot of our work is really hiring people for projects of how do they work on something for a longer period of time. And so that's, I think, one of the reasons that some of the traditional expert networks have struggled to get into this. And also how do you retain those people and think about all the incentives where it actually looks more similar in some ways to one of the traditional labor marketplaces of an Uber or DoorDash, just with much higher-skilled talent that's treated exceptionally well?
turns.zh: 确实如此。不过一个核心区别在于，AlphaSights通常是一次性服务，而我们的业务更多是为项目招聘人才，让他们长期投入工作。因此，我认为这也是一些传统专家网络难以切入这个领域的原因之一。此外，如何留住这些人才并设计激励机制，在某种程度上，这与Uber或DoorDash等传统劳动力市场平台非常相似，只不过吸引的是高技能人才，他们得到了格外优厚的待遇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's such a good opportunity for me to learn so much about this, so I'm going to ask questions.
turns.zh: 这对我来说是个绝佳的学习机会，所以我会多提问。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so interesting to me. How much of the experts are focused on specific concrete knowledge versus personality and softer skills? How much of it's like, "Here's how you do an exam. Here's how you do an x-ray"?
turns.zh: 这对我来说太有趣了。专家们专注于特定具体知识，还是更注重性格和软技能？比如，“这里是如何做考试的，这里是如何做X光检查的”？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: It depends on the lab. It's a lot of both. I think that previously it might've been more softer skills, but now a lot of the labs are focused on their business models of what are the economically valuable capabilities that drive revenue and leaning a lot into these professional domains. But I think the creative side is also still really important to everyone. And so we're seeing a meaningful amount of both. We hired all the people from the Harvard Lampoon a couple of months ago, their comedy club, to help with making models funnier. And so do all sorts of stuff like that, hiring Emmy award-winning screenwriters and everything across the board on creative capabilities that you'd look for.
turns.zh: 这取决于实验室。两者都有。我认为以前可能更多是软技能，但现在许多实验室专注于他们的商业模式，即哪些经济上有价值的能力能推动收入增长，并大力投入这些专业领域。不过我认为创造力对每个人来说仍然非常重要。因此，我们看到两者都占据重要地位。几个月前，我们从哈佛大学的喜剧俱乐部Harvard Lampoon招募了所有成员，帮助让模型更具趣味性。此外，我们还做了很多类似的事情，比如聘请艾美奖获奖编剧等等，涵盖了你能想到的各种创意能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is amazing. What a cool story. I'm excited for this to kick in. How fast do these things turn around? Say you hired this team, how fast are we going to see the impact potential? Is like months? Is it years?
turns.zh: 太棒了。真是个精彩的故事。我很期待这项技术能迅速落地。比如说，您聘请了这个团队，我们多久能看到潜在影响？是几个月？还是几年？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Well, so it depends, because some models or some labs will release iteratively where they'll just improve the model behind the scenes.
turns.zh: 嗯，这得看情况，因为有些模型或实验室会迭代式地改进模型——他们只是在幕后优化模型。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Without announcing a new model?
turns.zh: 那不发布新模型吗？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Exactly. Every couple of weeks versus others do these big releases. And so it depends a lot. We're behind all of them, but we move really fast. It would be a customer gives us a request of we need these award-winning screenwriters, and within 24 hours we'll turn around the experts. And then there's also this really interesting dynamic where in a set of 100 people that we hire, oftentimes the top 10% of people will drive majority of the model improvement. It's like a company. If you have 100-person company, oftentimes the top 10% of the company will drive majority of the impact. And what that means is that when we're able to build proprietary advantages in identifying who are those top 10% of people, both in so far as how do we have them on our platform but also identify and match them effectively, it creates so much value for customers that it's difficult to compete against. (00:36:08): And so it really does tie back to the founding thesis of the company, which is how do we find these extraordinary people and identify them so that we can reliably deliver these top 10% or top 10X experiences for our customers.
turns.zh: 没错。有些实验室每隔几周就会发布重大更新，而我们则要等很久。但这确实因人而异。我们落后于其他实验室，但我们的行动速度很快。比如客户提出需求，比如“我们需要这些获奖编剧”，我们就能在24小时内召集到专家。还有一个很有趣的现象：我们招的100个人中，往往前10%的人能推动模型改进的大部分工作。就好比一家公司，如果有100名员工，前10%的人往往能创造大部分价值。这意味着当我们能识别出这些前10%的人才——无论是如何将他们引入平台，还是有效地匹配资源——就能为客户创造巨大价值，让竞争者难以企及。（00:36:08）这确实与公司的创始理念相契合，即如何找到这些杰出人才并有效识别他们，从而为客户提供前10%甚至前10X级的体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So on that, so is the idea, you hire Jane. She's incredible at coding and she now works for Anthropic and that's her full-time job doing this? Or is this a part-time thing? Is this a project thing mostly?
turns.zh: 那就是说，比如你雇佣了简。她编程能力超强，现在在Anthropic工作，这是她的全职工作吗？还是兼职？或者主要是项目性质的？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: It would sometimes be part-time. Sometimes it would be full-time. I would say most often it's part-time where it's like someone might work at a thing company where they're underemployed, maybe one of the ones that's moving slower where they have an extra 20 hours a week and then they're able to do this on the side or whatever the equivalent is across a bunch of different industries. But we also do a lot of 40 hour a week roles as well.
turns.zh: 有时是兼职，有时是全职。我觉得大多数情况下是兼职。比如有些人在大公司工作但未能充分发挥潜力，他们每周可能有20小时的空闲时间，就能顺便做这个项目，或者在不同行业有类似的机会。但我们也有很多每周40小时的全职岗位。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And how much are they making? Is it meaningful enough for a AI engineer to spend time on this?
turns.zh: 那他们能挣多少钱？对AI工程师来说，投入时间做这件事是否值得？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Yeah, very meaningful. So our median pay rate in the marketplace is $95 an hour, but it can flex up, well up into $500 an hour based on the depth of someone's expertise. And one thing that highlights this difference relative to a lot of the crowdsourcing companies is if you look at the economics of the crowdsourcing companies, oftentimes they would pay $30 an hour to town as the average. And so think about the people that you can hire, the undergrads for $30 now versus the Goldman bankers, the McKinsey analysts, the Fang software engineers. And ultimately it comes down to what are the capabilities that labs want their models to have? And it much more falls in the latter bucket than the former one.
turns.zh: 非常值得。我们平台上的平均时薪是95美元，但根据专家的深度，报酬可以涨到500美元。与许多众包公司相比，这一差距很明显。众包公司的报酬通常只有30美元/小时。想想你能雇到的不同人才：30美元的本科生、300美元的高盛银行家、麦肯锡分析师、Facebook软件工程师。归根结底，关键在于实验室希望模型具备什么样的能力？而Anthropic在这方面比其他实验室做得好得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know there's only so much you can talk about with this stuff, but so Anthropic, Claude has been so good at coding so much better historically than other models. I also use it for writing, giving feedback on writing. What is it that allowed them to get so good at this and continue to be so good at this?
turns.zh: 我知道关于这些内容能透露的信息有限，但Anthropic的Claude在编程方面一直表现出色，比其他模型好得多。我也用它来写作、提供写作反馈。是什么让他们能如此出色并持续保持这种水平？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Well, I can't go too much into detail about customer work, but I think that it's this trend of reinforcement learning and being very thoughtful about defining the right rewards that we're releasing across the board. And how we could mitigate reward hacking, set up the right rewards, that's super impactful.
turns.zh: 嗯，我不能过多透露客户项目的细节，但我认为，当前强化学习的趋势，以及在定义合理奖励时保持深思熟虑的做法，正在我们整个团队中广泛推广。还有如何防范奖励被滥用、合理设定奖励机制，这些举措都产生了巨大影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Evals. Again, evals is all you need.
turns.zh: 还是回归到评估环节。再说一次，评估环节才是关键所在。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Back to evals.
turns.zh: 回到评估环节。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: One of my favorite quotes from customers is that, "Models are only as good as their evals," which has always held true.
turns.zh: 我最喜欢的客户名言之一是：“模型的质量取决于评估环节的质量。” 这一观点始终成立。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think Greg Brockman tweeted this once. "Evals are all you need."
turns.zh: 我记得格雷格·布罗克曼曾在推特上说过：“评估环节才是关键所在。”

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Yeah, truly.
turns.zh: 确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's talk about Mercor a little bit more. One of the maybe, not even maybe, I believe the data tells us it's the fastest growing company in history.
turns.zh: 让我们再多聊聊 Mercor 吧。Mercor 或许——甚至不只是或许——是史上发展最快的公司。数据告诉我们这一点。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to understand what you did to make this happen. So let me just ask, what do you think are some of the core tenets of how you built Mercor that most contributed to being this successful?
turns.zh: 我想了解你们是如何做到这一点的。所以我要问，你们认为在打造 Mercor 的过程中，最有助于取得成功的核心原则是什么？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: I think the most important thing is looking at the leading indicators in fast-moving markets. I remember when I used to think... Everyone in venture talks about the why now, and I used to think about the why now of how from a product standpoint, less from a market standpoint of now we can automate the way that we review resumes or the way that we conduct interviews, et cetera. But ultimately there is this legacy market that's has all these incumbents and it's relatively stagnant. But what matters a ton is actually figuring out what are the new markets, the new pockets of demand that are changing very quickly where the wealthiest customers in the world are willing to pay whatever it takes to improve model capabilities, and how do we focus on the leading indicators of those markets to make sure that we have the best solution for the flagship customers in the market and optimize everything around that. (00:40:18): And that's what I found has been most impactful in building the business. I think maybe that's one thing is leading indicators in markets. If I had to choose another, it's customer obsession. We have had for the last... We're starting to have a couple of product managers help out with go-to-market, but for the last year and a half of the business, we've had no one in sales and marketing. And so we're immature from a sales and marketing standpoint because we focused 100% of company resources on how do we build great products and experiences for our customers. Just getting word of mouth, the people that have worked with us at other businesses want to keep working with us and leaning into creating those great experiences. And so that's where I spend all my time. And I think that some founders can get caught up in how do they get really good at marketing before they've figured out the thing that really drives a lot of customer love and creates the six-star experiences that you're used to building.
turns.zh: 我认为最重要的是在快速发展的市场中关注领先指标。我记得我曾经认为……风险投资界都在谈论“为什么现在”，而我过去思考的是从产品角度看“为什么现在”，比如我们现在可以自动化简历审核流程、面试流程等等。但最终，传统市场存在诸多既有企业，发展相对停滞。但真正重要的是找到那些正在快速变化的新市场、新需求点，比如全球最富有的客户愿意不惜一切代价提升模型能力的市场。然后，我们要聚焦这些市场的领先指标，确保为市场中的头部客户提供最佳解决方案，并围绕这一核心优化所有环节。（00:40:18）这就是我在业务发展中发现最有效的策略。我认为核心原则之一就是关注市场领先指标。如果非要再选一个，那就是以客户为中心。我们过去一年半没有销售和市场团队，直到最近才引入几位产品经理协助市场推广。从这个角度看，我们在销售和市场方面还很不成熟，因为我们把公司所有资源都投入到如何为客户打造优质产品和体验上。口口相传自然而然，曾与我们合作过的客户都愿意继续合作，并致力于创造卓越体验。这就是我投入全部精力的地方。我认为有些创始人可能会陷入先精通营销的误区，而忽视了真正能激发客户热爱、创造六星级体验的核心要素。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to go back to that first point, which is like, okay, you found this pocket, maybe the biggest business opportunity in history. How did you first find... What was that moment of, "Wait, this could be really big"?
turns.zh: 我要回到第一个要点，也就是，你发现了这个商机，或许是史上最大的商业机会。那你是怎么最初发现的……当时你意识到“等等，这可能真的很重要”的那一刻是什么？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: So there's some crazy stories here. I remember we started the company as I mentioned in January 2023. And then in August 2023 when I was still in college, one of our customers introduced us to the co-founders of xAI over a Zoom call saying how we had these really smart Indian software engineers that were great at math and coding. So we met them and we explained how the software engineers we had were really good at math and coding because they weren't distracted by all the humanities. They didn't have to study history and English and all these other things, and they loved it. So they had us in two days later to the Tesla office and we met the entire xAI co-founding team except for Elon, while I was still a college student. And xAI was just getting started at that point and they were super excited about our focus on the quality of the experts. (00:42:22): And so while they were still doing pre-training, they weren't ready for human data at the time and we didn't start working with them at that point. We just knew from that point forward before we even dropped out that the market was about to change radically and we needed to be at the frontier of that. And so then fast-forward a few months, one of the crowdsourcing players came to us and actually used our platform to hire over 1,000 people where this is very interesting experience because we started getting flooded with support tickets about how those people weren't getting paid. And we obviously felt horrible because we had referred them to this opportunity. It was this reputable company. And we realized that a lot of the incumbents were resting on their laurels with respect to what was needed in the experiences they were creating for talent in their marketplaces to help improve models. And there was this opportunity to work directly with the labs in a way that kept the dignity of the experts in the marketplace, paid them extremely well, and cut out the middlemen. (00:43:31): And so we started doing that in May of last year, and then the rest is history.
turns.zh: 这里有些疯狂的故事。我记得我们公司是在2023年1月创立的，正如我之前提到的。然后在2023年8月，当时我还在上大学，我们的一位客户在Zoom通话中向xAI的联合创始人介绍了我们，称我们拥有非常聪明的印度软件工程师，他们在数学和编程方面很出色。所以我们见了他们，向他们解释说我们的软件工程师之所以擅长数学和编程，是因为他们不受文科课程的干扰。他们不必学习历史、英语之类的科目，他们热爱这份工作。结果两天后，他们就邀请我们去了特斯拉办公室，在那里我们见到了除埃隆以外的整个xAI联合创始团队，而那时我还是个大学生。当时xAI刚刚起步，他们对我们专注于专家质量的做法感到非常兴奋。（00:42:22）虽然他们当时还在做预训练，但还没有准备好使用人类数据，所以我们那时还没有开始与他们合作。但从那时起，甚至在退学之前，我们就知道市场即将发生巨大变革，我们需要站在变革的前沿。于是几个月后，一个众包平台找到我们，实际上是用我们的平台招聘了1000多人。这是一次非常有趣的经历，因为我们开始收到大量支持票，用户抱怨这些人没有得到报酬。我们显然感到很内疚，因为我们把他们推荐给了这个声誉良好的公司。然后我们意识到，许多现有公司在为市场上的人才创造提升模型所需的体验时，都满足于现状。我们看到了一个直接与实验室合作的机会，这样既能维护市场上专家的尊严，又能给他们提供极高的报酬，同时省去中间商。（00:43:31）所以从去年5月起，我们就开始这样做了，接下来的事就顺理成章了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, okay. Hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue since. So what I'm hearing here is you were very open to looking for poll. You saw some poll, you explored it. And then once you saw that there was something really meaningful there, you just went deep on making that an incredible experience as amazing as possible.
turns.zh: 哇，好，自那以后你们的营收达到了数亿美元。所以我听说你当时非常乐于寻找机会。你发现了一些机会，就去探索了。然后一旦你意识到这里面有真正有意义的东西，你就全力以赴地把它打造成尽可能出色的体验。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Exactly. I think if I had to distill it into advice for founders, one thing I've realized is that I spent a lot of time trying forced product-market fit. And in some ways you should be persistent. You should have these theses that you have conviction about how the world will change. But sometimes you just need to sheer it from the market and know that it's there, the poll, to know the right places to focus. Because if it's difficult to sell, if it's extremely difficult to sell the marginal customer, you're not going to be able to grow a huge business. What you actually need to find is the customer that's surprisingly easy to sell into where you're going to be able to grow with them. You know that it's a large pain point. And so it's some combination of being stubborn with respect to your thesis around how the world will change, but also very open-minded with respect to exactly what form that takes and how the market's developing and how your company will fit into it.
turns.zh: 没错。我觉得如果要给创业者提个建议的话，我意识到自己曾花大量时间去强行实现产品与市场的契合度。在某些情况下，你确实应该坚持不懈。你应该坚信世界将发生何种变革，但有时你只需顺势而为，了解市场动态，抓住关键机遇。比如，如果很难推销产品，特别是边际客户的转化极其困难，那么你就无法发展出大规模业务。相反，你需要找到那些令人惊喜的易推销客户群体，通过与他们合作实现增长。要知道，市场需求是巨大的痛点所在。因此，关键在于既要坚持自己对未来趋势的信念，又要保持开放的心态，顺应市场发展趋势，让公司能在其中找到立足之地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an amazing insight. In the moments you described, felt like it was a combination of this xAI meeting feeling like, "Oh wow, they really, really want this thing that we have. We're now doing an amazing job," and then it's 1,000 people hiring in the platform. Was that those two moments that are like, "Wow"?
turns.zh: 这真是个深刻的见解。在你描述的那些时刻，我感觉这既有种xAI会议上的感觉——“哇，他们真的非常需要我们开发的这个产品。我们现在做得太棒了”，又有平台上招聘1000人的那种震撼。难道这就是那种让人惊叹的时刻吗？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Exactly. And those happened, keep in mind, while we were a seed company, right? Well, so the first one was before we even raised any seed funding, we were totally bootstrapped because we bootstrapped the company to a million dollar revenue run rate and have always remained super capital-efficient. We've never burned money. We were lifetime profitable. And then we raised our seed round in September from General Catalyst, and it was the other experience after we raised our seed round where we really knew that there was an enormous amount of demand in this market where we saw the volume and we saw that the incumbents were sleeping with respect to how the market was changing and the kinds of people that were needed to make that change happen.
turns.zh: 没错。请记住，这些时刻发生在我们还是种子期公司的时候。第一件事是在我们甚至没有筹集到任何种子资金之前，我们完全是自力更生，因为我们把公司发展到年营收100万美元的水平，并且始终保持着极高的资本效率。从未烧钱，一直保持盈利。然后在9月份，我们从General Catalyst那里筹集了种子轮融资。筹集种子轮融资后的经历让我们真正意识到，这个市场存在着巨大的需求。我们看到了业务量，也看到了传统厂商对市场变化和推动变革所需人才的麻木不仁。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's one thing to see this opportunity and start to execute on it. It's another to actually succeed at this scale and consistently win. You guys have very specific values within the business. Talk about those. It feels like that's a big part of your success too.
turns.zh: 发现机遇并开始行动是一回事，但能在如此大规模上持续成功则完全是另一回事。你们公司内部有非常明确的价值观。能谈谈这些价值观吗？我觉得这也是你们成功的重要因素。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: It totally is. So I'll give the three and maybe a brief story associated with each of them. (00:46:10): So the first one is having a can-do attitude, which everyone gives me a little bit of a hard time for because it's a funny saying, but we've always set these ridiculously ambitious goals, and then somehow the trajectory of the company forms around those goals. Where I remember when we were talking to Benchmark before they led our Series A, we were at 1.5 million in run rate. And I said we'd be at 50 million in run rate by the end of the year. And they said we were absolutely insane, right, as anyone would. And plus or minus two weeks, we hit it. And then we've now well blown past the tracking to 500 million in run rate, which was initially our goal for this year. So setting these incredibly ambitious goals with respect to the revenue scale of the business, the caliber of experiences for talent, all those dimensions is super important to first have a can-do attitude. (00:47:04): The second thing is really high standards, which is who we hire and what we expect of them. We have an incredibly high hiring bar where we hire tons of former founders, people that have incredible experiences. We just hired or partnered with Sundeep Jain who joined us as president. He was previously the chief product officer and chief technology officer at Uber and joined our relatively small in the grand scheme of things company to help scale up all the processes where Uber is of course the largest labor marketplace in the world. So super high standards is of paramount importance. (00:47:41): And then the third one that we really lean on significantly is intensity. And that if you look at the early cultures of the legendary companies, thinking of Meta or Google, they have these incredible, intense early-stage cultures of people just moving heaven and earth and doing whatever it takes to push the frontier of model capabilities. And so still very much output-oriented of what do people achieve rather than input-oriented of the specific hours they work, but recognizing that it takes a lot to build a legendary business, and that's ultimately what we're optimizing for.
turns.zh:
确实如此。所以我会举三个例子，并简单讲讲每个例子背后的故事。（00:46:10）：第一个例子是拥有积极进取的态度。大家对此总有些微词，因为这听起来有点夸张，但我们一直设定那些看似疯狂的宏伟目标，然后公司的发展轨迹就会围绕这些目标展开。我记得在与Benchmark谈判A轮融资前，我们的营收规模是150万美元。我当时说年底前营收规模会达到5000万美元，他们当然觉得我们疯了，毕竟谁都会这么想。但最终我们提前两周就达成了目标。现在我们的营收规模已远超最初设定的年度目标，达到了5亿美金。所以，在营收规模、人才体验等维度设定极具挑战性的目标时，首先要具备积极进取的态度。

（00:47:04）：第二个关键点是高标准——这体现在我们招聘人才的标准和对他们的期望上。我们的招聘门槛极高，大量招募前创业者和拥有丰富经验的人才。我们刚聘请了Sundeep Jain担任总裁，他曾在Uber担任首席产品官和首席技术官，却选择加入我们这个相对规模较小的公司，帮助我们优化Uber作为全球最大劳动力市场的所有流程。可见，高标准至关重要。

（00:47:41）：第三个我们深信不疑的要素是激情。回顾传奇公司的早期文化，比如Meta和Google，他们都拥有令人惊叹的早期文化——员工们不遗余力地突破技术边界。这种文化高度以产出为导向，关注员工取得的成果，而非投入时间长短。但要记住，打造传奇企业需要付出巨大努力，而这正是我们不懈追求的目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I could see why this works. Can-do attitude plus high standards plus intensity, I could see how that leads to success. There's a lot of talk these days about this 6-9-9 culture, working six days a week, 9:00 AM to 9:00 PM. A lot of people are like, "Why? That's terrible. Why would you make people do that?" But at the same time, I'm just constantly hearing this from the most successful AI companies. This is just the way it is to be successful. Things are moving so fast. This is an opportunity you'll never see again. Just talk about your thoughts on that.
turns.zh: 我能理解为什么这种模式行得通。积极进取的态度、严苛的标准和激情，我能理解它们如何共同促成成功。如今人们常谈论6-9-9文化，即每周工作六天，每天从上午9点到晚上9点。但很多人会问：“为什么？这太糟糕了。为什么要让员工这样做？”但与此同时，我不断从最成功的AI公司听到这种说法。这就是成功的秘诀。事物变化太快了。这是一个难得的机会。谈谈你对此的看法吧。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Yeah. Well, to clarify, we've never mandated hours. It's more been a byproduct of people that care a lot where we care a lot about the trajectory of the business. And so a lot of people come into the office and stay late. But if they need to leave early and get dinner with their kids or travel on the weekend, of course that's totally fine. And for us, it's much more about finding people who have a lot of ownership and are really bought in, less so about the specific hours in the office, even though we found that oftentimes it's the people that are most bought in, not always, but oftentimes it's the people that are most bought in and that burn the midnight oil with us.
turns.zh: 是的。需要说明的是，我们从不强制规定工作时间。这更多是员工自身对公司发展轨迹高度关注的结果。因此很多人会来办公室加班到很晚。但如果他们需要早退去和孩子共进晚餐，或者周末出差，我们当然完全支持。对我们来说，关键在于找到有主人翁意识、全身心投入的人，而不是拘泥于具体的工作时间。不过我们发现，最投入的人往往也会和我们一起通宵工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you say high standards, is there something you could share that gives us an example of what you mean there? Because a lot of people think they have high standards and they don't.
turns.zh: 您提到高标准，能否举个例子让我们更清楚您的意思？因为很多人自认为有高标准，但实际上并非如此。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: If you are very patient, there's always some trade-off between speed and quality when hiring. And I remember especially for our first 10 people, we were just so patient and disciplined about finding some of the best people in the world. Half of them are... Our second employee, Sid, as an example, our second employee in the US, Sid was previously the head of growth at Scale who joined us when we were a seed stage company. Daniel who joined us was previously scaled to consumer apps to over 100,000 users and all sorts of just extraordinary backgrounds of our first 10 hires. And I think that that initial talent density shaped so much of what the rest of the org looks like as you scale it up.
turns.zh: 如果您非常有耐心，那么在招聘时，速度和质量之间总会有权衡取舍。我记得尤其是在我们招聘前10位员工时，我们非常耐心且自律，力求招到世界上最优秀的人才。他们中有一半……比如我们的第二位员工Sid，在美国的第二位员工Sid，此前是Scale公司的增长部门主管，当时我们还是一家种子期公司。他加入我们后，Daniel也加入了我们，Daniel此前曾将消费类应用扩展至10万用户以上——我们前10位员工都有着非凡的背景。我认为最初的人才密度极大地影响了公司后续的发展方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know you also have this perspective that people talk about waiting to hire, to hire really slowly, but it's actually not necessarily the right advice. Talk about that.
turns.zh: 我知道您也持有这种观点，即人们常说要慢慢招聘，但这未必是正确的建议。能否谈谈这一点？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: It's painful because it's a double-edged sword. On one hand, I'm thrilled that our first 10 people are so phenomenal and I think that that has paid dividends for the business. But on the other hand, I think that companies do get to the point where you just need to hire really fast. And there's some things where you need a lot of people to do them and you need to recognize that there's going to be some variants associated with hiring, but moving quickly is the priority. (00:51:07): And I think that in some ways, we move too slowly with how we scaled out the team. And so the benefit is that everyone is extraordinary. We have this super high bar and we want to maintain that over time. But I think the downside is that while the company has grown incredibly quickly, we likely could have grown even faster if we had moved a little bit more quickly with especially ramping from call, like 10 to 100 people.
turns.zh: 这很痛苦，因为它是一把双刃剑。一方面，我为前10位员工如此出色而感到兴奋，我认为这为公司带来了回报。但另一方面，我认为公司确实会到一个必须快速招聘的阶段。有些工作需要大量人手来完成，你必须承认招聘过程中会有变数，但快速行动是优先事项。（00:51:07）：我认为在某种程度上，我们在团队扩展方面进展得太慢了。好处是每个人都很出色。我们设定了极高的标准，并希望长期保持这一水平。但我认为缺点是，虽然公司增长极快，但如果我们能更快地扩展团队，特别是从10人扩展至100人，或许本可以发展得更快。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, I was going to ask. So it sounds like the first 10, be very careful, take your time, 10 to 100, maybe speed up a bit.
turns.zh: 好的，我正想问。听起来前10位员工要非常谨慎，慢慢来，10到100人，或许可以加快速度。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Yes, though I wouldn't say it's necessarily 10. It's determined by the point where you know it's really working. And I know that's still not a bright line, but it's like once you know that there's so much more demand than you can handle, that's when you want to step on the gas and optimize for speed in a lot of ways. But I think especially until then, it's important to be patient, be disciplined. Get the best people is always important, but speed becomes more important once you find the market opportunity, the market vacuum.
turns.zh: 是的，但不一定是10人。关键在于何时知道招聘策略真的有效了。我知道这没有明确的界限，但一旦你发现需求远超现有能力时，就该加速并以多种方式优化速度了。但在此之前，保持耐心和自律至关重要。招到最优秀的人始终重要，但一旦发现市场机遇、市场空白，速度就变得更加重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know you've started a couple companies in the past, much smaller scale. In this new role as CEO of this massive hyper growth company, what surprised you most about where you spend the time most or just what the role involves? Because a lot of people want to start companies dream about being in your shoes. What are they maybe not understanding about where a lot of your time goes?
turns.zh: 我知道您过去创办过几家规模小得多的公司。作为这家高速增长的大型公司的CEO，您最惊讶的是什么？您花最多时间在哪里？或者说这个角色涉及哪些方面？因为很多人想创业，梦想着能像您一样。关于您大部分时间花在哪里，他们可能不了解的方面是什么？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Yeah, it's actually not too surprising. The top two buckets are always working on hiring and time with customers of how do I really deeply understand what customers need and how we can support them? And then how do I build the team and a lot of the processes around that? Of course, there's all of the ad hoc things I didn't expect of dealing with the people questions of how do we set up our levels and our comp bands and all of that, which you learn as you scale a business. But I think that the core places that I spend my time are in line with what I expected as well as what I love doing, which is very fortunate.
turns.zh: 是啊，这其实并不意外。前两项工作重点始终是招聘和客户沟通——如何深入理解客户需求，如何为他们提供支持？然后是如何组建团队以及相关流程。当然，还有许多临时应变的工作，比如处理员工关系、设定职级和薪酬区间等，这些都是在企业发展过程中逐渐摸索的。但我认为，我投入精力最多的核心领域既符合我的预期，也符合我的兴趣所在，这真是幸运之事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So these two companies you've started in the past, maybe share what they work because they're fun, and then how do they help you be successful in this? What's something that they taught you that helped you in your current role?
turns.zh: 你之前创办的两家公司，能否分享一下它们的成功之道？它们为何有趣？又如何助力你如今的事业？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Yeah, so there's been like a dozen, but I'll choose my favorite two. So when I was in eighth grade, I started Donut Dynasty where I saw that Safeway Donuts were selling for $5 a dozen, and I was amazed because I felt like as an eighth grader, this was such an incredible deal. And I started to bike down to Safeway, buy Safeway Donuts for $5 a dozen, and then go back to my middle school and then sell them for $2 each, running really good margins of course. It sold out super quickly. And so then I need to scale up. So I would pay my mom $20 to drive me in her minivan down to Safeway, buy 10 dozen donuts, go to my middle school, sell them all out. (00:54:19): And then the school tried to shut me down because I was selling food on school campus, which they didn't like. So they had me in the principal's office asking me to not do that. And then I moved my donut stand over 50 feet, so it was off school campus, saying that they could no longer police me. I remember we had competitors pop up where the competitors were charging. They bought these Chuck's Donuts, which if anyone in the Bay Area knows, are higher end donuts than Safeway Donuts, but they have a higher cost basis. They cost a dollar per. And so I dropped my prices to $1 for two weeks to run them out of business before I knew what anti-competitive practices were. And I'd hire all my friends, paying my friends in donuts because they perceived the donuts as $2 each where they could sell them throughout the school and I could have a lower cost basis on them. (00:55:12): So I had all of these fun experiences in selling donuts, and then I could talk more about my high school business as well, which was a more significant scale. But I think the takeaway from that was just like you can just do things. So many people have ideas, but the barrier to more companies being built, I think, is just initiative and taking the steps to build the product or experience that customers want and investing the time and the ambition to scale that up. And so I think it was really getting reps of that that enabled me to realize that I should do it later on at a much larger scale.
turns.zh: 嗯，创办的公司有十来家吧，但我最喜欢的两个是Donut Dynasty和另一家教育科技公司。Donut Dynasty的故事很有趣。八年级时，我发现Safeway超市的甜甜圈每打5美元出售。这让我觉得作为八年级学生，这价格太划算了。于是我骑自行车去Safeway买一打，然后回中学以每个2美元的价格售卖，利润空间自然很大。很快就卖光了。后来我需要扩大规模，就花20美元雇妈妈开小面包车去批量采购，再卖到学校。（00:54:19）但学校不让，因为校园内不允许售卖食品。于是我把摊位移到校外50英尺外，声称超出校园管辖范围。还有竞争对手出现，他们卖Chuck's Donuts。湾区的朋友都知道，Chuck's Donuts比Safeway的品质高，但成本也更高，每个1美元。我把价格降到2美元一对，迅速击败对手。当时我还雇了朋友帮忙，朋友觉得每个2美元能在校园卖出，而我的成本更低。（00:55:12）这些卖甜甜圈的趣事让我受益匪浅。高中时期的商业项目规模更大，但最重要的启示是行动力至上。许多人有想法，但创业的核心在于主动行动，打造客户真正需要的产品或体验，并投入时间和精力将其规模化。我想正是这些实践经验让我后来意识到，应该以更大规模去践行这些理念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing story. I love how wholesome that is versus drugs, selling donuts.
turns.zh: 真是个精彩的故事。比起毒品贩卖，卖甜甜圈多健康啊。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Then my mom was very worried. She was like, "Oh, is there any pot of these donuts?" I was like, "No, mom, I assure you these are pure donuts."
turns.zh: 然后我妈特别担心，问：“这些甜甜圈里有大麻吗？”我说：“没有啊，妈，我向你保证都是纯甜甜圈。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you paid your mom $20 to drive.
turns.zh: 我喜欢你花20美元雇妈妈开车去采购的做法。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Yeah. She was adamant it couldn't be a handout that she was taking her time to drive me, so she needed to make a little bit of money off of it. We haggled over her title where eventually she wanted to be head of global operations, which we found very entertaining.
turns.zh: 是啊。她坚称这不是免费帮忙，她花时间开车送我，所以得赚点钱。我们还讨价还价了她的职位头衔，最后她想当全球运营总监，我们觉得这很有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I hope that's on her LinkedIn.
turns.zh: 希望她把这段经历写进领英。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Not yet. Maybe she'll have to add it.
turns.zh: 还没呢。可能她得加进去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you said that you've started a dozen companies?
turns.zh: 你说你创办了十几家公司？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Okay.
turns.zh: 哇。好吧。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Well, a dozen projects, but I think it was that, and then my AWS company were the two that I scaled up.
turns.zh: 嗯，十几个项目吧，但我觉得主要是我创办的两家公司，AWS公司和Mercor。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the story behind Mercor as the name?
turns.zh: Mercor这个名字有什么含义吗？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Mercor means marketplace in Latin or to buy, sell, trade. And we want to build the largest marketplace in the world, the marketplace for how everyone finds jobs, and that was really the draw to it.
turns.zh: Mercor在拉丁语里是“市场”的意思，或者是“买卖、交易”的意思。我们想打造全球最大的市场平台，让每个人都能在这里找到工作，正因如此，这个名字才这么吸引人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, maybe a last question. This is going back to earlier in discussion because it's something I've been thinking about as we're talking. There's been this shift from data as the fuel for models, and now it's experts. Do you think there's a next step, or is this just will take us to AGI, superintelligence?
turns.zh: 好的，最后一个问题。回到之前的讨论，因为我们聊的时候我一直在思考这个问题。数据从模型的燃料变成了专家的燃料，你觉得下一步会是什么？还是说这只会把我们带向通用人工智能（AGI）和超智能？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: I don't think it's necessarily changing from data to experts. It's more just the paradigm of realizing that labs need this close collaboration with experts to help understand what are the evals that they're building and how can they push the frontier. But I think it's very clear that evals are evergreen, that so long as we want to improve models, we'll need experts to create evals for them and to create the post-training data for them to learn those capabilities. And of course there might be changes in the exact way that people do training with RL or otherwise, but they will always need an eval to measure what does success look like across every domain that they want to build.
turns.zh: 我觉得不一定是从数据到专家的转变。更重要的是，要意识到实验室需要与专家密切合作，这样才能理解他们正在构建的评估模型，以及如何突破技术前沿。但我认为很明显，评估模型是永不过时的，只要我们想改进模型，就需要专家为它们创建评估模型，并为它们提供训练后数据，以学习这些能力。当然，人们可能在RL等训练方式上会有一些变化，但每个想构建的领域都需要评估模型来衡量成功标准。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So then building on that, a question that comes up a lot these days is, and I know we're talking about fun stuff but I'm getting to serious stuff again, scaling laws and just progression of model intelligence. A lot of people are feeling like, "I don't know, it's slowing down. We're not going to really get to superintelligence at this rate." What is your sense?
turns.zh: 好的。那基于这一点，最近经常被提到的议题是，尽管我们在讨论有趣的事情，但我还是要回到严肃的话题——缩放定律和模型智能的进步。很多人觉得“我不知道，进展太慢了。按照这个速度，我们永远也达不到超智能。”你怎么看？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: I totally agree with that. I know there's been some executives to big labs that say we'll have superintelligence in three years, but I think the truth is that it's a longer road. And that's not to diminish from how extraordinary the models are. I think we'll be able to automate a majority of knowledge work tasks in the next 10 years for sure, but that long road is paved with all of the evals that help to make those capabilities possible. And it's not going to be 10X more pre-training data that gets those capabilities. It's much more going to be all of the post-training data sets that are far more data-efficient and thoughtful that help us get there.
turns.zh: 我完全同意这个观点。我知道有些大实验室的高管说三年内就能实现超智能，但我认为事实上这是一条更漫长的道路。这并不是要贬低现有模型的非凡之处。我认为未来10年我们肯定能让大多数知识型工作自动化，但这条漫长道路的基石是所有帮助实现这些能力的评估模型。并不是需要10倍更多的预训练数据来获得这些能力，而是需要更多训练后数据集，这些数据集数据效率更高、设计更合理，帮助我们实现目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: David Sachs tweeted this interesting point that the situation we're now is almost the best case scenario where AI is not in this fast takeoff to superintelligence. There's a lot of competitors keeping each other in check. Models are already very valuable and only getting valuable, more valuable, but there's not just this winner superintelligence taking over the world situation.
turns.zh: 大卫·萨克斯在推特上提出了一个有趣的观点：我们目前所处的局面几乎是人工智能尚未迅速发展至超智能的最佳情况。目前有众多竞争者相互制衡。模型已经非常有价值，且价值还在不断提升，但并非只有一个超级智能主宰世界的局面。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Yeah, I think that's true. I think a lot of the super intelligence fearmongering is probably overrated, but at the same time a lot of people's framing around that is even if there is a 5 to 10% chance of this P-Doom, then we should be careful, which seems logical. But I think that it's going to be an extraordinary 10 years for all of Silicon Valley and all of the world as this technology is able to create abundance and giving everyone better medical treatment, the best access to legal recommendations, and the ability to build great products more than we've ever seen before.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为这确实没错。我觉得对超智能的恐惧可能被过度渲染了，但与此同时，很多人对此的看法是，即便存在5%到10%的末日灾难风险，我们也应该保持谨慎，这似乎合乎逻辑。但我认为未来十年对整个硅谷和全球来说都将是非凡的，因为这项技术能够创造财富，为每个人提供更好的医疗服务，让人们更便捷地获取法律建议，并比以往任何时候都更能创造出优质产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And education feels like is transforming.
turns.zh: 教育领域似乎也在发生变革。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Absolutely, right. I even have felt bits of this over the last 10 years where I remember ever... My parents would give me a hard time for not going to classes in college and I'd be like, well, there's way better lectures on YouTube. Why not just listen there? But I can only imagine as the models get extremely good at conveying information, better than the best professor, what that'll mean and access to all sorts of information to better forward humanity and upskill everyone.
turns.zh: 确实如此。过去十年里，我也亲身感受到了这一点。我记得以前父母总因为我大学不去上课而责备我，我就说，那YouTube上有更好的讲座，为什么不去听呢？但我只能想象，随着模型在传递信息方面变得极其出色，甚至比最优秀的教授还要好，这将意味着什么，以及获取各种信息来推动人类进步和提升每个人技能的可能性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I'll use that as a segue to a final question. I'm going to take us to AI Corner, which is a recurring segment on the podcast. What's some way that you personally use AI to do better work to help you in life?
turns.zh: 接下来我要把话题转到AI Corner，这是播客的一个固定环节。您个人是如何利用AI来提高工作效率、改善生活的？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Well, let's see. I use it a lot to write documents, as you would expect. I also talk to get advice on problems. I find it helpful to just reason through almost as a thought partner because, yeah, I don't know. I find I think better sometimes when I'm talking something through, but I can't talk through everything with colleagues or people around me.
turns.zh: 嗯，让我看看。我经常用它写文档，这很显然。我也会用它来寻求问题的建议。我发现把问题讲出来思考，几乎就像和一个思维伙伴交流一样很有帮助，因为，有时候我也不知道该怎么想。有时候把问题讲出来，我能更好地理清思路，但我不可能和同事或身边的人把所有问题都讲出来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so this is like ChatGPT Voice Mode mostly or something else.
turns.zh: 那主要是用ChatGPT的语音模式还是其他方式？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Yeah, I like ChatGPT Voice Mode a lot. There's stuff-
turns.zh: 是的，我很喜欢ChatGPT的语音模式。还有一些其他功能——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Me too.
turns.zh: 我也是。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: ... or room for improvement, but I am very excited about the future of Voice.
turns.zh: ……或者说还有改进的空间，但我对语音技术的未来非常兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me show you something I built, actually. I wasn't planning to talk about this, but there's this guy, Eric Antonow, who's been recommended by a lot of people to get him on this podcast. He's this creative product person that's under the radar now. He's at Facebook for a long time. He built this project called Pirate GPT, which is you basically put ChatGPT into a stuffed animal to talk to it. So built a little wise owl. I don't have it on right now.
turns.zh: 让我给你们展示一下我开发的东西，实际上我本来不打算讲这个的，但很多人推荐埃里克·安东诺夫上播客。他是一个现在不太受关注的创意产品人。他在Facebook工作了很久。他开发了一个叫Pirate GPT的项目，基本上就是把ChatGPT装进一个毛绒玩具里，让它能和人对话。所以他做了一个小猫头鹰。我现在没把它带过来。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But basically you sew in a little speaker right here and you put a little magnet underneath and you can put it on your shoulder and then you just talk to it.
turns.zh: 但基本上你只要在这里缝进一个小扬声器，在下面放一个小磁铁，就可以把它戴在肩上，然后和它对话了。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: That's so cute. Wow. I love it. I'll have to get one of those. Because I have some of the voice assistants in my apartment, but I really want a ChatGPT voice assistant, so I'm excited for-
turns.zh: 太可爱了。哇。我喜欢这个。我也得去买一个。因为我公寓里已经有一些语音助手了，但我真的很想拥有一个ChatGPT语音助手，所以我对此特别期待——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was just thinking that. Yeah, just come on. Why can't we have a ChatGPT voice just sitting around listening to us all the time. And you can't on your phone because it goes to sleep and it's like, "Hello, what?"
turns.zh: 我刚也在想这个。是啊，说真的，为什么我们不能有一个ChatGPT语音助手一直坐在那里听我们说话呢？用手机的话，它会进入睡眠模式，然后说：“喂，你说什么？”

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Exactly. Yeah.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, so it's what this is trying to be. Well, there's a kickstarter he started that we'll link to that. You could help out.
turns.zh: 是啊，所以这就是他们努力打造的方向。嗯，他发起了一个Kickstarter项目，我们会把链接放出来，大家可以支持一下。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: There we go.
turns.zh: 好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's really easy. (01:02:25): Brendan, is there anything else that you wanted to share or touch on or maybe leave listeners with before we get to a very exciting lighting round?
turns.zh: 这真的很简单。（01:02:25）：布伦丹，还有什么想分享、探讨或者给听众留下印象的吗？在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Tying to the point around initiative and that you can just do things, I encourage everyone, especially with AI and it being so much easier to build, just take the initiative to go out and build products and talk with customers and take that leap of faith because I think that that is in so many ways, the largest barrier to more innovation, the economy in any way that we can support that.
turns.zh: 回到主动性这个话题，以及你可以直接行动起来这一点，我鼓励大家，尤其是面对AI技术，开发起来变得如此容易的时候，就主动去开发产品、与客户交流，抓住这个机遇。因为我认为，从很多方面来说，这是推动创新和经济发展的最大障碍，我们需要尽可能地支持这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. There's so many people that just, let's not bash the podcast, but just listen to podcasts, read posts, just keep reading and listening and don't do anything with that information. And there's never been an easier time to actually build stuff and try stuff.
turns.zh: 是啊。太多人只是——不是说要贬低播客，但他们只是听播客、读帖子，然后就停留在信息层面，从不付诸行动。现在真正开发产品和尝试新事物的机会从未如此容易。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So definitely take that advice. Just you can do things. You can move your donut stand 50 feet and get out of their jurisdiction.
turns.zh: 所以一定要听从这个建议。只要你能行动起来。你可以把甜甜圈摊移到50英尺之外，离开他们的管辖范围。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, Brendan, with that, we've reached a very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好的，布伦丹，我们现在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节了。我有五个问题要问你。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: All set.
turns.zh: 准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 你最近最常向别人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Let's see. I would say in order, High Output Management is a phenomenal book on running companies. Second is Zero to One, which of course is a classic. And then third is Shoe Dog, where I just find it to be a really inspirational story.
turns.zh: 让我想想。首先是《高效能管理》，这是一本关于公司管理的杰出著作。其次是《从0到1》，这无疑是一本经典之作。第三是《鞋狗》，我觉得这是一个非常鼓舞人心的故事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a recent movie or TV show you really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 你最近看过或者很喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: I really liked Oppenheimer. My favorite TV show of all time is Suits, so I know not recent, but if I had to choose a recent one, probably Oppenheimer.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢《奥本海默》。我最喜欢的电视剧是《金装律师》，所以我知道这不是最近的，但如果非要选一部最近的，我可能会选《奥本海默》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very cool. Suits, first time someone's mentioned that. Favorite product you recently discovered that you really love?
turns.zh: 太酷了。《金装律师》，这是第一次有人提到它。你最近发现的最喜欢的产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: I love using Codex, like the new version. I know it's sort of new in terms of version. Yeah, I think it's incredible and just a huge, huge improvement. So yeah.
turns.zh: 我喜欢用Codex，新版本的。我知道它在版本上还算新的。是的，我觉得它太棒了，进步巨大。真的很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a life motto that you find yourself coming back to, sharing with folks, finding useful in work or in life?
turns.zh: 你有没有一条人生格言，让你反复回味、与人分享、在工作或生活中觉得很有用？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: I think it's you can just do stuff, what we were talking about earlier. Take the leap of faith.
turns.zh: 我觉得你可以直接行动，就像我们之前讨论的那样。勇敢迈出信念的一步吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I thought you were going to say can do, which is in your Twitter profile.
turns.zh: 我以为你要说"can do"（能做到），这在你的推特简介里有提到。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Can do as well, yeah.
turns.zh: "Can do"当然也可以，哈哈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Two great ones. Final question. So we were chatting before this about things that we could talk about and you shared this interesting thing that you haven't shared anywhere else, which is that you're dyslexic. Why don't you share that with folks? And just how do you get around that having built the fastest-growing company in history?
turns.zh: 这两个都很棒。最后一个问题。我们之前聊到可以谈论的话题，你分享了一个很有趣的细节——你有阅读障碍。为什么不跟大家分享呢？还有，你是如何克服这个障碍、创立了史上发展最快的公司呢？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: I don't hide it at all. I think a lot of my colleagues know. And I think on one hand it definitely makes it difficult to go through 1,000 emails a day or read every document that I'm supposed to, but on the other hand, I feel like it helps me to think a little bit differently, to be more creative, and perhaps see that markets are changing that not everyone sees. And so it's turned out okay so far. And so I think one thing it's helped me realize from a management standpoint is that we focus much more on how we can leverage people's strengths rather than helping to improve weaknesses, because there's some things that I'm not great at and I'll never be the best in the world at, and there's others that I can hopefully refine and strive to be.
turns.zh: 我一点也不隐藏这个事实。我觉得很多同事都知道。确实，处理每天上千封邮件、阅读所有需要阅读的文件会比较困难，但另一方面，我觉得这让我能以不同的视角思考问题，变得更有创造力，也许能发现别人没注意到的市场变化。到目前为止效果还不错。从管理角度来看，我意识到我们更应该关注如何发挥员工的优势，而不是纠结于改进他们的弱点，因为有些事情我做得不好，永远也比不上世界上最优秀的人，但有些方面我可以努力提升和改进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such a also recurring theme on this podcast of just focusing on strengths and not focusing over all your focus on weaknesses. (01:05:53): Brendan, this was incredible. I learned so much. I have a billion more questions, but you got shit to do. Two final questions. What should people know about what you're doing and roles you're hiring for? And then how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 这也是本播客反复强调的主题——专注于优势，而非过度关注弱点。（01:05:53）：布伦丹，这次访谈太棒了。我学到了很多，还有无数问题想问，但你还有事要忙。最后两个问题：你应该让人们了解你的业务和招聘职位吗？听众如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Absolutely. We're hiring a ton across the board on our team. We're hiring strategic project leads on our operations team, software engineers in our engineering team, as well as researchers. And so please go to mercor.com and we would love to work with you, and that's the largest way that you can help us. Share it with your friends as well. Over half of people in our marketplace come from referrals because we have a platform of people that love us. And so any jobs that you want to apply to or send your friends to, we would love to have you.
turns.zh: 当然！我们团队正在大规模招聘。运营团队需要战略项目负责人，工程团队需要软件工程师，还有研究员。请访问mercor.com，我们期待与你合作。这是能帮助我们最有效的方式，也请转发给朋友们。我们市场上的用户中，有超过一半是通过推荐来的，因为我们拥有一群热爱我们的用户群体。任何你想申请的职位或推荐给朋友的，我们都欢迎。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Brendan, thank you so much for joining me.
turns.zh: 布伦丹，非常感谢你接受采访。

turns.speaker: Brendan Foody
turns.en: Thank you for having me.
turns.zh: 感谢邀请我。
